Rosenberg's goanna (Varanus rosenbergi) exhibits a maximum aerobic metabolic scope that reflects its active foraging lifestyle. Respirometry trials conducted on field-fresh individuals at a body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] recorded a maximal basal oxygen consumption of 4.7325 milliliters per minute [JOi = 4.7325 milliliters per minute], a value that aligns with the elevated metabolic demands of a large, wide-ranging Varanid predator. This measurement, derived from flow-through respirometry on post-absorptive animals, underscores the species' capacity for sustained pursuit of prey across the sclerophyll forests it inhabits. The comparatively high resting metabolic rate, measured under the same thermal conditions, was somewhat lower at 3.1 milliliters per minute [JOi = 3.1 milliliters per minute], suggesting a substantial factorial aerobic scope that permits prolonged activity without entering anaerobic debt at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. These metabolic data, collected during the austral summer when animals are most active, provide a critical baseline for understanding the energetic constraints on the species' life history, particularly in relation to its reproductive output and the thermal dependence of its physiological performance.

Sexual maturation in female Rosenberg's goanna occurs after an extended period of post-hatching development, with individuals attaining puberty approximately three years after hatching [tp = approximately three years after hatching] when maintained at a stable thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This estimate, drawn from comparative datasets on the congener Varanus bengalensis, suggests a relatively slow pace of maturation consistent with the species' large body size and K-selected life-history strategy. Following the attainment of reproductive maturity, females typically produce a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year] during the spring breeding season, with clutch sizes ranging from 10 to 14 eggs [N_R_i = clutch sizes ranging from 10 to 14 eggs]. The annual reproductive rate is therefore modest when averaged over the entire year, reflecting the significant energetic investment each clutch represents. This low fecundity is compensated by a relatively high degree of parental investment in nest site selection and thermoregulation of the incubating eggs, behaviors that enhance hatchling survival in the thermally challenging environments of southern Australia.

Neonatal Rosenberg's goannas emerge from the egg at a remarkably modest size, with hatchlings weighing approximately 26 grams [Wwb = approximately 26 grams] immediately following egg tooth emergence, based on published data for the related Nile monitor (Varanus niloticus). This body mass represents a precipitous drop from the adult asymptotic weight, which can reach 2654.38 grams [Wwi = 2654.38 grams], indicating that individuals must undergo a dramatic increase in mass of over one hundred-fold over the course of their lives. Such extreme ontogenetic scaling in body size imposes significant demands on the juvenile growth phase, during which hatchlings must acquire sufficient prey to fuel both somatic expansion and the accumulation of lipid reserves for overwintering. This initial low mass at birth may also render the yolk-sac larvae vulnerable to predation and desiccation, pressures that likely select for rapid growth rates and the early achievement of a body size that exceeds the gape limits of many sympatric predators.

The developmental timeline of Varanus rosenbergi is strongly influenced by incubation temperature, with the period from oviposition to hatching being particularly sensitive to thermal conditions. When eggs are incubated at a constant temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the embryonated eggs require approximately 335.5 days [ab = approximately 335.5 days] to complete development, a remarkably protracted incubation that far exceeds that of most squamate reptiles and reflects the species' adaptation to the cool, temperate climate of its island strongholds. This extended incubation at low temperatures may allow the hatching event to be timed with the onset of favorable spring conditions, when invertebrate prey becomes abundant. By contrast, the maximum recorded longevity for this species, estimated at 22 years [am = 22 years] based on demographic comparisons with the Bengal monitor (Varanus bengalensis) at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], indicates that once individuals survive the attrition-prone early life stages, they enjoy a relatively long reproductive lifespan that can offset the low annual fecundity through repeated breeding attempts across multiple decades.

Comparative life-history analyses place Varanus rosenbergi at the slow end of the lizard fast-slow continuum, with its maximum lifespan of 22 years [am = 22 years] under warm thermal conditions (25 °C [T = 25 °C]) being several times greater than that of many similarly sized varanids from tropical regions. The species' reliance on a relatively low annual reproductive output, characterized by a single clutch of 10 to 14 eggs per year [Ri = 10 to 14 eggs per year] with only one nesting event each year [F_R_i = one nesting event each year], is consistent with this slow-paced life history. The substantial investment per offspring is further evidenced by the long incubation period, which at cool temperatures can require over eleven months for completion, and the modest hatchling mass of 26 grams [Wwb = 26 grams] that necessitates a prolonged juvenile phase before reproductive maturity is attained at three years after hatching [tp = three years after hatching] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This suite of life-history traits—extended development, delayed maturation, high adult survival, and low annual fecundity—is typical of insular reptile populations facing unpredictable resource availability and high juvenile mortality, and it underscores the vulnerability of this species to anthropogenic disturbances that disproportionately impact older, reproductively active cohorts.
